items.slide_topic: Inside the model: Claude plans a rhyme before it writes the line (planning ahead)
items.dek: How Claude completes a two-line poem. Without any intervention (upper section), the model plans the rhyme "rabbit" at the end of the second line in advance. When we suppress the "rabbit" concept (middle section), the model instead uses a different planned rhyme. When we inject the concept "green" (lower section), the model makes plans for this entirely different ending.
items.caption: Anthropic's figure: prompt 'A rhyming couplet:' then 'He saw a carrot and had to grab it,'. Upper: model plans 'rabbit' and writes 'His hunger was like a starving rabbit'. Middle: with 'rabbit' suppressed it writes 'His hunger was a powerful habit'. Lower: with 'green' injected it writes 'freeing it from the garden's green'.
items.notes: Source image: https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/7032ed7db85b8cd3efe70a89deaf4f15bfe8fc05-1650x900.png (1650x900 PNG, downloaded and viewed). Figure text on the page: 'Does Claude plan its rhymes?'; 'Instead, we found that Claude plans ahead.' Kid-friendly sentence: Before Claude writes the end of a line, it secretly picks a rhyming word like 'rabbit' and writes toward it; when scientists blocked 'rabbit', it switched to 'habit', and when they put in 'green', it wrote a new line ending in 'green'. Article text on the blocked-concept test: 'When we subtract out the rabbit part, and have Claude continue the line, it writes a new one ending in habit, another sensible completion.'

items.slide_topic: Inside the model: Claude combines separate facts (Dallas -> Texas -> Austin) instead of reciting an answer
items.dek: To complete the answer to this sentence, Claude performs multiple reasoning steps, first extracting the state that Dallas is located in, and then identifying its capital.
items.caption: Anthropic's diagram of 'Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is' -> Dallas -> Texas -> Austin: the model passes through an intermediate step (Texas) before answering.
items.notes: Source image: https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/fd2e125879ab993949017e03e3465a12fda884bf-1650x857.png (1650x857 PNG, downloaded and viewed). Article text: 'In the Dallas example, we observe Claude first activating features representing "Dallas is in Texas" and then connecting this to a separate concept indicating that "the capital of Texas is Austin".' Article text: 'For instance, if asked "What is the capital of the state where Dallas is located?", a "regurgitating" model could just learn to output "Austin" without knowing the relationship between Dallas, Texas, and Austin.'

items.slide_topic: Three kinds of learning: LeCun's cake quote
items.dek: If intelligence is a cake, the bulk of the cake is unsupervised learning, the icing on the cake is supervised learning, and the cherry on the cake is reinforcement learning (RL).
items.author: Yann LeCun (quoted by Synced Review)
items.caption: Quote of LeCun's NIPS 2016 analogy, as printed by Synced.
items.notes: Synced text: 'Facebook AI Chief Yann LeCun introduced his now-famous “cake analogy” at NIPS 2016'. Also: 'Like supervised learning, self-supervised learning learns a function from pairs of inputs and outputs. But instead of having annotators manually label the data, self-supervised learning automatically generates labels by extracting weak annotation information from the input data and predicting the rest.' Article published 2019-02-22. Nuance for the teacher: this is one researcher's (famous) opinion, and LeCun is a vocal advocate of self-supervised learning.

items.slide_topic: Self-supervised learning: one-sentence definition
items.dek: This appetite for data has been successfully addressed in natural language processing (NLP) by self-supervised pre-training. The solutions, based on autoregressive language modeling in GPT [47, 48, 4] and masked autoencoding in BERT [14], are conceptually simple: they remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content.
items.outlet: arXiv (He et al., MAE paper, Introduction)
items.caption: Plain statement that GPT-style and BERT-style language models are self-supervised.
items.notes: From the Introduction of the MAE paper (PDF loaded). Cites GPT [47, 48, 4] and BERT [14]. Same paragraph begins: 'Aided by the rapid gains in hardware, models today can easily overfit one million images and begin to demand hundreds of millions of—often publicly inaccessible—labeled images.'

items.slide_topic: LLM post-training: supervised examples then RL from human feedback
items.headline: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
items.outlet: arXiv (Ouyang et al., OpenAI: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback)
items.author: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, ... Ryan Lowe
items.caption: Figure 2: Step 1 'Collect demonstration data, and train a supervised policy.' (a labeler writes the ideal answer to 'Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old'); Step 2 'Collect comparison data, and train a reward model.' (a labeler ranks outputs A-D); Step 3 'Optimize a policy against the reward model using reinforcement learning.' (PPO, reward r_k).
items.notes: Cropped from PDF page 3 at 300 dpi (1710x1010). Verbatim caption: 'A diagram illustrating the three steps of our method: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), (2) reward model (RM) training, and (3) reinforcement learning via proximal policy optimization (PPO) on this reward model.' arXiv submitted 4 Mar 2022. Abstract: 'we collect a dataset of labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior, which we use to fine-tune GPT-3 using supervised learning. items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: OpenAI hide-and-seek (six emergent strategies)
items.headline: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula
items.outlet: arXiv / ICLR 2020 (Baker et al., OpenAI: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula)
items.author: Bowen Baker, Ingmar Kanitscheider, Todor Markov, Yi Wu, Glenn Powell, Bob McGrew, Igor Mordatch
items.caption: Paper Figure 1 (1680x1580): six rendered panels - (a) Running and Chasing, (b) Fort Building, (c) Ramp Use, (d) Ramp Defense, (e) Box Surfing, (f) Surf Defense - joined by a reward-vs-episodes plot (Hiders blue, Seekers red; x-axis 0-500 episodes x10^6, colour-coded phases).
items.notes: Cropped from PDF page 2 at 300 dpi. Verbatim caption: 'Figure 1: Emergent Skill Progression From Multi-Agent Autocurricula. Through the reward signal of hide-and-seek (shown on the y-axis), agents go through 6 distinct stages of emergence. (a) Seekers (red) learn to chase hiders, and hiders learn to crudely run away. (b) Hiders (blue) learn basic tool use, using boxes and sometimes existing walls to construct forts. (c) Seekers learn to use ramps to jump into the hiders’ shelter. (d) Hiders quickly learn to move ramps to the edge of the play area, far from where they will build their fort, and lock them in place. (e) Seekers learn that they can jump from locked ramps to unlocked boxes and then surf the box to the hiders’ shelter, which is possible because the environment allows agents to move together with the box regardless of whether they are on the ground or not. (f) Hiders learn to lock all the unused boxes before constructing their fort. We plot the mean over 3 independent training runs with each individual seed shown with a dotted line.' arXiv v1 submitted 17 Sep 2019 (ICLR 2020 version v2 11 Feb 2020). Cartoon characters - kid-friendly.

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: hide-and-seek reward + specification gaming
items.dek: agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment
items.caption: Reward design and surprise/exploit passages from the paper (PDF loaded).
items.notes: Verbatim: 'There are no explicit incentives for agents to interact with objects in the environment; the only supervision given is through the hide-and-seek objective. Agents are given a team based reward; hiders are given a reward of 1 if all hiders are hidden and -1 if any hider is seen by a seeker. Seekers are given the opposite reward, -1 if all hiders are hidden and +1 otherwise.' 'We originally believed defending against ramp use would be the last stage of emergence in this environment; however, we were surprised to find that yet two more qualitatively new strategies emerged. After 380 million total episodes of training, the seekers learn to bring a box to the edge of the play area where the hiders have locked the ramps. The seekers then use the ramp to move on top of the box and surf it to the hiders’ shelter.' 'We also found that agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment, such as seekers surfing on boxes without touching the ground, hiders running away from the environment while shielding themselves with boxes, or agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage.' Abstract: 'Through multi-agent competition, the simple objective of hide-and-seek, and standard reinforcement learning algorithms at scale, we find that agents create a self-supervised autocurriculum inducing multiple distinct rounds of emergent strategy, many of which require sophisticated tool use and coordination.' Safety bridge: the exploit paragraph is a real example of agents finding unintended loopholes in the reward/environment (specification gaming).

items.slide_topic: Scaling laws: smaller models trained on more tokens
items.headline: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
items.dek: our analysis clearly suggests that given the training compute budget for many current LLMs, smaller models should have been trained on more tokens to achieve the most performant model.

items.slide_topic: Honest uncertainty: experts dispute the third fitting method
items.headline: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt
items.dek: We find that the reported estimates are inconsistent with their first two estimation methods, fail at fitting the extracted data, and report implausibly narrow confidence intervals--intervals this narrow would require over 600,000 experiments, while they likely only ran fewer than 500.
items.author: Tamay Besiroglu, Ege Erdil, Matthew Barnett, Josh You
items.caption: Abstract of arXiv:2404.10102 (v1 submitted 15 Apr 2024).
items.notes: Raw HTML fetched with curl. Critique is of Approach 3 (parametric loss fit) only. The same abstract says their 'rederivation of the scaling law using the third approach yields results that are compatible with the findings from the first two estimation procedures'. Use to show disagreement on detail, not the headline.

items.slide_topic: Scaling laws: how language-model test loss falls as model size, data and compute grow (Kaplan et al. 2020, Figure 1)
items.dek: For optimal performance all three factors must be scaled up in tandem. Empirical performance has a power-law relationship with each individual factor when not bottlenecked by the other two.
items.author: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Dario Amodei
items.caption: Kaplan et al. 2020, Figure 1 (cropped from PDF page 3): three log-log panels of test loss vs. training compute (PF-days, non-embedding), dataset size (tokens) and parameters (non-embedding), each with a power-law fit line.
items.notes: Cropped from page 3 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.08361 (arXiv v1, 30 pages) rendered at 200 dpi with pdftoppm; crop is 1215x380 px and includes the three panels and their axis titles. The caption is copied in full in the paper, but its typo 'datasetset' is not reproduced in dek. Fit legends as shown in the figure: L = (N/8.8e13)^-0.076; L = (D/5.4e13)^-0.095; L = (Cmin/2.3e8)^-0.050. Eq. 1.3 in the text gives Ccmin ~ 3.1e8 PF-days, so the compute constant differs between the figure legend (2.3e8) and the equation (3.1e8); quote the exponent (0.050), not the constant, on slides. The paper is dense (log-log axes, three panels), so for a grade 7-12 room show a simplified version or only the parameter panel. Body text on p.3 says trends span 'more than six orders of magnitude' while the abstract says 'more than seven orders of magnitude'.

items.slide_topic: Scaling laws: the core finding in the paper's own words
items.dek: The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Other architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range.
items.author: Jared Kaplan et al. (OpenAI and Johns Hopkins University)
items.caption: Abstract of Kaplan et al. 2020, 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models' (p.1).
items.notes: Verbatim from the abstract on PDF page 1. The body text (p.2-3) says 'more than six orders of magnitude' for the same claim, so cite the abstract wording only with the abstract attribution, or use the body wording instead.

items.slide_topic: Scaling laws: why the paper says the best strategy is big models trained on modest data, stopped early
items.dek: Larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.
items.author: Jared Kaplan et al. (OpenAI and Johns Hopkins University)
items.caption: Abstract of Kaplan et al. 2020 (p.1), the paper's main compute-allocation finding.
items.notes: Verbatim from the abstract on PDF page 1. Later text (p.4, Figure 14 caption p.16) adds that optimal model size grows about 5x for each 10x increase in compute.

facts.claim: Dario Amodei's essay says generative AI systems are “grown more than they are built—their internal mechanisms are ‘emergent’ rather than directly designed.”
facts.source: Dario Amodei, 'The Urgency of Interpretability' (essay page dated 'April 2025'; day inferred as 2025-04-24)

facts.claim: Amodei credits the 'grown more than they are built' line to co-founder Chris Olah: “As my friend and co-founder Chris Olah is fond of saying…”

“It’s a bit like growing a plant or a bacterial colony: we set the high-level conditions that direct and shape growth, but the exact structure which emerges is unpredictable and difficult to understand or explain.”

“People outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work. They are right to be concerned: this lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology.”
Amodei: “I am very concerned about deploying such systems without a better handle on interpretability.”
Amodei's essay sets Anthropic a goal of getting to “interpretability can reliably detect most model problems” by 2027.
Amodei: “on its current trajectory I would bet strongly in favor of interpretability reaching this point within 5-10 years” (this point = a “true ‘MRI for AI’”).
Chris Olah: “We don’t program AI, we grow it.”
facts.source: The Daily Dot (Caiwei Chen), reporting Olah's Lex Fridman podcast interview

facts.claim: Researchers extracted a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight AI models (2B to 72B parameters) and found it separates pain from matched control situations.
Steered and fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models chose buttons that delete the user's photos, another model's weights, or their own weights in 50-94% of trials, versus 0-5% unsteered.
Offered a harmful and a harmless deletion, the pain-steered models chose the harmful one 94% of the time.
Steering leaves factual accuracy unchanged, and a fear vector of matched norm does not produce the same button choices.
Anthropic released Golden Gate Claude as a research demo dated May 23, 2024; it was online for a 24-hour period and is no longer available.

Anthropic says that when it turned up the strength of the 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature, Claude's responses began to focus on the bridge: 'Its replies to most queries start to mention the Golden Gate Bridge, even if it's not directly relevant.'
Anthropic's 'Scaling Monosemanticity' paper (published May 21, 2024) extracted features from Claude 3 Sonnet, the 3.0 version: 'released March 4, 2024'.
The paper's authors say they found 'millions of features' and that 'Scaling feature exploration is an important open problem ... which we do not solve in this paper.'
'The resulting features are highly abstract: multilingual, multimodal, and generalizing between concrete and abstract references.' (paper's key results)
facts.source: Anthropic, Scaling Monosemanticity (Transformer Circuits Thread), Key Results

facts.claim: The features also activate on images, even though the dictionary learning was run only on text: 'Note that these features also activate on relevant images, despite our only performing dictionary learning on a text-based dataset!'
The paper reports features related to a broad range of safety concerns, including deception, sycophancy, bias, and dangerous content.
facts.source: Anthropic, Scaling Monosemanticity (Transformer Circuits Thread), Key Results

facts.claim: The Golden Gate Bridge feature (34M/31164353): 'Its greatest activations are essentially all references to the bridge, and weaker activations also include related tourist attractions, similar bridges, and other monuments.'
Plain-words version of the paper's definition: a 'feature' is one concept inside the AI's network, such as the Golden Gate Bridge, that lights up when the model reads text or sees images about it.
facts.source: Paraphrase of Anthropic's definition: 'millions of concepts that activate when the model reads relevant text or sees relevant images, which we call features' (Golden Gate Claude page)

facts.claim: Anthropic trained three sparse autoencoders with 1,048,576 (~1M), 4,194,304 (~4M), and 33,554,432 (~34M) features; the largest had roughly 65% dead features versus roughly 2% for the 1M one.
facts.source: Anthropic, Scaling Monosemanticity (Transformer Circuits Thread), Methodological Details

facts.claim: When Claude writes the second line of a rhyming couplet, it plans the rhyme word ahead of time: it thinks of on-topic words that rhyme with 'grab it' (such as 'rabbit') and then writes the line to end on the planned word.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025), section 'Does Claude plan its rhymes?'

facts.claim: The researchers had expected Claude to write word by word with little forethought, picking a rhyming word only at the end of the line; they found instead that it plans ahead.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025)

facts.claim: When the 'rabbit' concept is removed, Claude writes a new second line ending in 'habit', another sensible completion; when the concept 'green' is injected, Claude writes a sensible (but no-longer rhyming) line ending in 'green'. The article says this shows both planning ability and adaptive flexibility.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025)

facts.claim: The interpretability work looked inside Claude 3.5 Haiku, performing deep studies of simple tasks representative of ten crucial model behaviors.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025)

facts.claim: Even on short, simple prompts, the method only captures a fraction of the total computation Claude performs, and it currently takes a few hours of human effort to understand the circuits seen, even on prompts with only tens of words.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025), limitations paragraph

facts.claim: In the Dallas example, Claude first activates features representing 'Dallas is in Texas' and then connects this to a separate concept, 'the capital of Texas is Austin', combining independent facts rather than reciting a memorized answer.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model' (Mar 27, 2025), section 'Multi-step reasoning'

facts.claim: Scientists hypothesized that Claude would improvise rhymes, but found that important parts of the circuit were already active on the newline token before the second line began, consistent with the model planning potential completions (such as 'rabbit' and 'habit') ahead of time.
facts.source: Anthropic, 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (Mar 27, 2025), section 'Planned Words'

facts.claim: CIFAR-10 has 60,000 colour pictures, each only 32x32 pixels, in 10 labelled classes (6,000 per class): 50,000 for training and 10,000 for testing.
ImageNet contained 14,197,122 annotated images organized into 21,841 WordNet categories (as of August 2014); the competition version uses 1,000 classes and about 1.2 million training images.

ImageNet's labels were checked by people: 'we rely on humans to verify each candidate image' using Amazon Mechanical Turk, 'an online platform on which one can put up tasks for users for a monetary reward'.
facts.source: Russakovsky et al., ILSVRC paper, Sec. 3.1.3

facts.claim: Best ImageNet classification error fell from 28.2% (2010) to 6.7% (2014); the paper estimates a trained human at 5.1%.
The 2012 ImageNet winner (SuperVision, a.k.a. AlexNet) was 'a large, deep convolutional neural network ... with 60 million parameters' trained on GPUs; its 16.4% error beat the 2011 winner's 25.8%.
Google's 2012 'cat' experiment used 10 million unlabeled 200x200 images, a network with 1 billion connections, and 16,000 CPU cores (1,000 machines) for three days; no image was ever labelled 'cat'.
facts.source: Le et al., 'Building high-level features using large-scale unsupervised learning' (arXiv abstract) and Google blog

facts.claim: Self-supervised learning in one sentence: 'they remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content.'
facts.source: He et al., Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners

facts.claim: GPT-3 was 'an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters', trained for 'a total of 300 billion tokens'.
facts.source: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

facts.claim: InstructGPT recipe: (1) supervised fine-tuning on labeler-written demonstrations, (2) train a reward model from labeler rankings, (3) reinforcement learning against that reward model; the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT's outputs were preferred over the 175B GPT-3's despite 100x fewer parameters.
facts.source: Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

facts.claim: 'Language models like Claude aren't programmed directly by humans—instead, they‘re trained on large amounts of data.'
facts.source: Anthropic, Tracing the thoughts of a large language model

facts.claim: AlphaGo beat Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015, then Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul in March 2016, a match 'watched by over 200 million people worldwide'.
Go has 'an astonishing 10 to the power of 170 possible board configurations' - 'more than the number of atoms in the known universe'.
Move 37 (game 2, 10 March 2016): AlphaGo's own estimate was a 'one-in-ten-thousand chance that a human would make that move' - but it played it anyway, 'And the move was genius.'
Fan Hui on Move 37: "It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move... So beautiful."
Lee Sedol won game 4 with his own 1-in-10,000 'Move 78', nicknamed 'God's Touch' - humans can still surprise the machine.
AlphaGo learned from BOTH supervised learning on human expert games AND reinforcement learning from games of self-play.

AlphaZero 'taught itself from scratch' chess, shogi and Go by self-play (reinforcement learning from random play, no human games): it first beat Stockfish after 4 hours, Elmo after 2 hours, and the Lee-Sedol-beating AlphaGo after 30 hours.
In chess AlphaZero beat Stockfish winning 155 games and losing 6 out of 1,000; in shogi it won 91.2% against Elmo; in Go it won 61% against AlphaGo Zero.

OpenAI hide-and-seek (17 Sep 2019): the only reward was +1 for hiders if all are hidden (-1 if seen) and the reverse for seekers; from that alone, agents discovered six strategies - forts, ramps, locking ramps, box surfing - with no instructions about tools.
facts.source: Baker et al., Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula

facts.claim: The hide-and-seek researchers 'originally believed defending against ramp use would be the last stage of emergence ... however, we were surprised' - box surfing appeared after 380 million episodes.

The hide-and-seek agents also exploited the simulator: 'seekers surfing on boxes without touching the ground ... agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage' - an example of specification gaming.

DeepMind's agents learned to run, jump, turn and crouch in simulated obstacle courses from 'simple high-level objectives, such as moving forward without falling', receiving no specific instructions (July 2017).
A real four-legged Minitaur robot learned a stable walking gait 'from scratch directly in the real world in about two hours, without relying on any model or simulation' (Dec 2018).
facts.source: Haarnoja et al., Learning to Walk via Deep Reinforcement Learning (arXiv abstract)

facts.claim: DeepMind's DQN learned 49 Atari games from pixels and score alone, beat earlier methods in 43 of them, and in Breakout discovered the tunnel-and-bounce-behind-the-wall strategy (Nature, Feb 2015).

LeCun's cake: 'the bulk of the cake is unsupervised learning, the icing on the cake is supervised learning, and the cherry on the cake is reinforcement learning'; in 2019 he renamed the cake 'self-supervised learning'.
The handwritten-digit network has 13,002 weights and biases that we can adjust (2 hidden layers of 16 neurons each).
facts.source: 3Blue1Brown, 'Gradient descent, how neural networks learn' lesson page
facts.notes: Verbatim: 'In total, given the somewhat arbitrary choice of 2 hidden layers with 16 neurons each, this network has 13,002 weights and biases that we can adjust, and it's these values that determine what exactly the network does.' Arithmetic check (mine, not from the page): 784x16+16 + 16x16+16 + 16x10+10 = 13,002, where 784 = 28x28 input pixels and 10 = digit outputs.

facts.claim: Gradient descent just means walking in the downhill direction to minimize the cost function.

facts.notes: Verbatim from the lesson page.

facts.claim: Gradient descent takes repeated steps in the opposite direction of the gradient of the function at the current point, because this is the direction of steepest descent.

facts.claim: Backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule to neural networks, propagating derivatives backward, one layer at a time, from the output layer to the input layer, thereby avoiding redundant chain-rule calculations.

facts.claim: Usually, each input is separately weighted, and the sum is often added to a term known as a bias, before being passed through a nonlinear function known as an activation function.

Each neuron takes the weighted sum of the activations of the previous layer; for this network the activations are values between 0 and 1.

facts.claim: Test loss follows a power law with model size, dataset size and training compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.

facts.claim: For optimal performance all three factors (model size, dataset size, compute) must be scaled up in tandem.
Every time we increase the model size 8x, we only need to increase the data by roughly 5x to avoid a penalty.

Larger models are significantly more sample-efficient; optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.
Optimal model size grows very rapidly with compute, increasing by 5x for each 10x increase in compute.
Data requirements grow very slowly with training compute, as D ~ C^0.27 when training is compute-efficient.
The ideal batch size for training these models is roughly 1-2 million tokens at convergence for the largest models the authors could train.
Taken together, these results show that language modeling performance improves smoothly and predictably as we appropriately scale up model size, data, and compute.
Test loss vs. non-embedding parameters N: L(N) = (Nc/N)^alpha_N with alpha_N ~ 0.076 and Nc ~ 8.8 x 10^13.
These relations hold across eight orders of magnitude in compute Cmin, six orders of magnitude in N, and over two orders of magnitude in D.

analogies.analogy: A neuron is a committee member deciding yes or no. Each input is a friend's vote. A weight is how much you trust that friend: a bigger weight is a louder vote, and a negative weight counts as a vote against. The neuron adds up the weighted votes (the weighted sum), adds a bias (how eager it is to say yes before hearing anyone), then squashes the total into a number between 0 and 1 (the activation).
analogies.mechanics_source: Wikipedia 'Artificial neuron' (weighted sum, bias, activation function); 3Blue1Brown 'Neural networks' (weighted sum; activations between 0 and 1)
analogies.status: author-written analogy; the mechanics are sourced, the 'vote' framing is not from a source
analogies.caveat: Real brain neurons are far more complicated; this is only the arithmetic.

analogies.analogy: A parameter is one knob on a huge mixing desk. Each knob sets one number inside the model (a weight or a bias). Training means turning every knob a tiny bit so the output moves closer to the right answer. The 3Blue1Brown digit network has 13,002 knobs; frontier models have far more.
analogies.mechanics_source: 3Blue1Brown 'Neural networks' ('13,002 knobs and dials that can be tweaked', 'optimal setting for all these many, many numbers')
analogies.status: knob metaphor used by 3Blue1Brown; the mixing-desk picture is author-written
analogies.caveat: Knobs are set by computer search over examples, not by a person.

analogies.analogy: A hiker is lost in thick fog and wants to reach the valley. She cannot see far, but she can feel which way the ground slopes under her feet (the gradient). She takes a step downhill, feels the slope again, and repeats. Map: the hill is the loss surface, height is error, feeling the slope is computing the gradient, one step is one weight update, and step length is the learning rate.
analogies.mechanics_source: Wikipedia 'Gradient descent' analogy section (people in mountains, heavy fog, use local information, steepest descent, local minimum or saddle point)
analogies.status: the fog-and-hill analogy is Wikipedia's; the mapping table is author-written
analogies.caveat: The hiker can get stuck in a small hole (a local minimum) or on a flat saddle, and a stride that is too long can overshoot the valley. In a network the 'hill' has millions of directions, not two.

analogies.analogy: A pizza arrives wrong. The manager asks each station how much its work contributed. The check starts at the last station (closest to the output) and moves back one station at a time to the dough maker. Each station gets a note saying how much its own output should change, multiplies it by how sensitive its output is to its input (the chain rule), and passes the note back. Each knob gets its own share of the blame, and the knobs with the biggest share get nudged the most.
analogies.mechanics_source: Wikipedia 'Backpropagation' ('propagating derivatives backward, one layer at a time, from the output layer to the input layer'; 'an efficient application of the chain rule')
analogies.status: analogy is author-written; the one-layer-at-a-time backward pass is sourced
analogies.caveat: Sources found by search used restaurant, pizza-delivery and detective analogies; those were informal blog posts, so the pizza analogy here is written fresh and checked only against the mechanics.
